## §12 — How people actually run these with less fast memory

`26:11` → `29:17` · 14 beats · 403 words · 186s · `12-how-people-actually-run-these.md`

| at | say | where | what happens |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `26:11` | The mistake in our last plan was not offloading. It was pretending we had to fetch every selected expert from the slowest place, every single time. Real systems can be smarter than that. The simplest improvement is a cache. Keep some expert weights in fast memory. | the paper stage | the empty shelf from §11 fills with a few expert blocks |
| `26:31` | When the router asks for an expert that is already there... that is a hit. No long trip needed. | the paper stage | a requested block is already on the shelf and makes a short hop |
| `26:41` | If the expert is not there... that is a miss. Then you fetch it from slower memory or storage, use it, and decide what should stay close. | the paper stage | the next request is absent, travels the long way, and lands in the cache |
| `26:53` | And systems can get smarter still. They can move experts between levels of memory. They can overlap transfers with computation. | the paper stage | several requests run quickly, some short and some long |
| `27:02` | And some approaches try to predict or prefetch experts before the router fully needs them. So yes: you can run a large MoE model without keeping every weight in the fastest memory. | the paper stage | a faint second path starts a block moving before it is asked for |
| `27:16` | But now we have a trade. | the paper stage | a slider appears between store and compute, sitting in the middle |
| `27:19` | Keep more experts close... and you need more fast memory, but you fetch less. | the paper stage | dragged one way the shelf grows and long trips thin out |
| `27:27` | Keep fewer experts close... and the machine can fit into less fast memory, but you risk more misses and more waiting. | the paper stage | dragged the other way the shelf shrinks and the machine slows |
| `27:38` | So where is the perfect setting? This is where I do not want to fake certainty. | the paper stage | the slider returns to the middle and stops, with nothing resolving it |
| `27:45` | It depends on the hardware. It depends on the workload. And it depends on how predictable and repetitive the expert choices actually are. | the paper stage | the things the answer depends on appear around the slider |
| `27:55` | For smaller MoE architectures, expert locality and caching have been measured and exploited. What we can say is that GLM has: 288 routed experts × 42 sparse layers = 12,096 layer-specific expert slots. | the paper stage | the routing geometry ghosts in behind the slider |
| `28:31` | Only eight routed experts are selected in each sparse layer for a token... but which eight matters for what has to be nearby next. | `28:50` | You can use less fast memory. You can offload. You can cache. You can quantize. You can shard the model across devices. But every one of those choices changes the performance trade. | the paper stage | the machine keeps running while the options are labelled around it |

## §13 — What “18 billion active” actually buys

`29:17` → `32:41` · 13 beats · 411 words · 204s · `13-what-that-number-bought.md`

| at | say | where | what happens |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `29:17` | Here is the payoff. When you read: 320 billion parameters and 18 billion active — those two numbers are answering different questions. The 320 billion tells you how many learned parameters exist in the model. The 18 billion active tells you roughly how much of that parameter set participates in the computation for a token. | the paper stage | `320B total` returns above `18B active` and two brackets are drawn |
| `29:43` | And that is the trick Mixture of Experts is buying you. The model can have a huge pool of learned expert weights... without running every expert for every token. | the paper stage | the whole model draws as a field with small active paths lit across it |
| `29:56` | For our it, the router only selected eight routed experts on each sparse layer. Another token can use a different route. Another sentence can use a different route. | the paper stage | our own `it` route replays quickly up the sparse floors |
| `30:08` | So the model gets access to far more total learned capacity than it has to compute through on every single token. That is the win. | the paper stage | the frame splits: total stays full while only the work side shrinks |
| `30:19` | But notice what it does not magically do. It does not turn a 320-billion-parameter checkpoint into an 18-billion-parameter file. The experts that are inactive for this token still exist. Another token may need them later. | the paper stage | the unused pool stays present around the route, labelled available |
| `30:37` | So if you want the whole model fully resident in fast memory, total stored weights and their precision still matter enormously. | the paper stage | stored weight and precision return as the thing that sets the footprint |
| `30:48` | And now our opening comparison stops being weird. This model: gpt-oss-120b uses roughly 4.4% of its parameters per token and ships at roughly 58 GiB in its compact MXFP4 format. | the paper stage | the exact two model cards from §1 return and the left one is measured |
| `31:06` | This model: GLM-5.3-Flash uses roughly 5.6% per token, but its shipped FP8 checkpoint is roughly 306 GiB before runtime memory. | the paper stage | the right one is measured the same way |
| `31:21` | Similar active percentages. Completely different total footprints. That difference is not some mysterious failure of MoE. They are different-sized models stored at different precisions. And “percent active” was never the number that told us the checkpoint size. | the paper stage | three quiet cause cards land between them |
| `31:37` | So when you see a model advertised as: 320B total — 18B active — read it like this: 320B total: how much learned model exists. 18B active: roughly how much participates for each token. | the paper stage | everything collapses back to one card with a meaning under each number |
| `31:55` | And if someone turns that second number into: “so you only need 18 billion parameters in memory”... now you know exactly what question to ask: which 18 billion — and when does the model know? | the paper stage | the opening question returns, put to the viewer rather than the screen |
